finding.claim: DELETE /projects/:id performs no authorization. authorized() returns a boolean whose result is discarded, so any authenticated non-owner non-admin can delete any project.

trace.note: authorized(req.user, project) evaluated; boolean result ignored, no throw

finding.guards_checked: authorized() at api.js:12-14 returns boolean and is not enforced at line 18. PUT handler uses authorize() which throws, so handlers are inconsistent. No ownership middleware visible in this file; if router-level middleware enforces ownership on this route the finding is mitigated, but none was visible.

verdict.guard_found: authorized() at api.js:12-14 returns a boolean, and its result is discarded at api.js:18, so it enforces nothing. The only enforcing check, authorize() at api.js:4-10, throws, but it is called only from the PUT handler at api.js:25, not on the DELETE route. No router-level or ownership middleware is visible; the directory contains only api.js.
verdict.reason: api.js:18 calls authorized(req.user, project) as a bare statement, so its false result has no effect, and req.store.projects.delete(project.id) at api.js:19 runs for any caller whose req.user is set; the PUT handler at api.js:25 uses the throwing authorize() instead, so the DELETE route is missing the check. The one caveat is that the mount point and auth middleware that populate req.user are not in this directory, so the attacker is an authenticated low-privilege user only if upstream auth is applied to this router.

finding.claim: Unknown project ids cause an unhandled TypeError (500) instead of 404, creating an existence oracle. On PUT, 403 for existing-but-not-owned versus 500 for nonexistent reveals which ids exist.
finding.sink: resource.ownerId dereference of undefined at api.js:5 and api.js:13

trace.note: store.projects.get(id) returns undefined for nonexistent id
authorize(req.user, undefined) reads undefined.ownerId, TypeError; existing unowned project yields 403 at api.js:5-8

finding.guards_checked: No if(!project) guard in either handler. No error handler visible to normalize the 500.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are the ownership tests at api.js:5 and api.js:13, and they run after the dereference, so they never guard against an undefined resource. No `if (!project)` check exists at api.js:17 or api.js:24, and no error handler appears in api.js. Express's default handler turns the thrown TypeError into a 500.
verdict.reason: For PUT, a nonexistent id makes api.js:24 return undefined and api.js:5 throw a TypeError (500), while an existing project not owned by the caller hits the 403 at api.js:6-7, so the status code reveals which ids exist. The trace is accurate. The attacker only needs a normal authenticated account, since the bug is reachable with any req.user. Impact is limited to id enumeration, and that is low severity if ids are unguessable. Separately, api.js:18 discards the boolean returned by authorized(), so DELETE at api.js:19 removes any project regardless of owner. That is a more serious authorization bypass than the one this candidate reports, and it should be filed on its own.

finding.claim: PUT rename stores req.body.name with no type or length validation. Exploitability depends on downstream consumers, which are not visible.
finding.sink: project.name assignment at api.js:26, returned via res.json at api.js:27

trace.note: authorize() gates the write correctly for owner or admin

finding.guards_checked: authorize() at api.js:25 gates the write. No schema or type validation in this file. If no body parser is mounted, req.body is undefined and throws a TypeError. Parser and downstream consumers not verified.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:4-10 is called at api.js:25 and throws a 403 on failure, so the throw aborts the handler before the assignment at api.js:26. Its call is a bare statement, but it is a throw-based guard, so the discarded return value does not matter. authorized() at api.js:12-14 is a different, bool-returning function and is not called on this route.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at api.js:25-27 match the candidate, but the only user who can reach the write at api.js:26 is the owner or an admin (authorize() at api.js:5 throws otherwise), and that user already controls the name field, so nothing in this file gives an attacker more power. Any harm would come from unseen downstream rendering of the name, which the candidate itself says is not visible, so there is no demonstrated vulnerability here.
